more of a VP?

>And occasionally, someone will actually try and withdraw
>'cause they are out of a deck, and sometimes it even works, which is always

PTOing all of someone's vampires can be hysterical too, I don't see this an

first place.

and, in the absence of a time limit, it's easy enough for the judge to declare
a stalemated situation.

The ability for someone to get a VP without ousting anyone, creates more
options for carving up tables, something routinely considered to be against the
spirit of the game.

>But it is really hard to withdraw. You need cooperation, generally, from the

>hand, it does allow a group of players all dug in and unwilling to lunge the
>ability to agree to mutually withdraw and all get out with a single VP
>(which is easily better than sitting stuck till time runs out and then
>getting .5 VPs).

Just tacking on to a random post, mainly.

I don't *like* the "Let's just sit here and discard until we withdraw
and get a VP each" situation. It feels wrong. However, it is currently
the best play in the game in a number of situations. So, I've just dug
up something I wrote a month ago. The main thing it's missing is
Brinksmanship - but then, I'm concerned about that card in general
anyway.

***
A more useful tack - if such [[edit: people mutually withdrawing]] is a
problem - is to provide a series of disincentives. For instance, it
might be worth considering the implications of withdrawal not being
worth a full VP. For instance, were it worth only half a VP, there
would be no difference between it and timing out. In such an instance,
it would be worth playing to the end in case you could oust someone,
since withdrawing now would gain you nothing over timing out at the end.
(Unless one of the people likely to die is you. But if you're that
precarious, the other people on the table may have something to say
about allowing you to withdraw instead.)

Of course, there are several knock-on effects so such a proposal might
not be perfect. [[edit: it would mean that currently legitimate
withdrawal was also penalised, say]]

Alternative proposals might be to, say, have any ties resolved by
withdrawals counting after non-withdrawals. So if you have 1 TW, 9 VPs
(a sweep and two twos) and I have a 1 TW, 9 VPs (a sweep and two twos)
*but* in one of my games I withdrew to get the two VP and we're tied
for last place into the finals (small tournament)... I lose, you get in.

This then makes more aggressive gains of VPs count "better" than
withdrawals. You then don't have to ban the deal itself. A
withdrawal is an inherently worse way to gain a VP than a
non-withdrawal/oust, then. [[edit: I'm not sure that this is bad. It's
social engineering, yes, but I tend to think that aggressive (in the
sense of ousting their prey) decks should probably be rewarded]]

Alternatively again, you might want to look at the withdrawal rule
itself. If you decide you wanted to keep it (which you might not),
you might want to change it. Picking a random idea from my Big Hat Of
Random Ideas, only the first player to withdraw from a game receives a
VP. Someone who has a legitimate need to get the hell out of the game
can get a VP that way. But then it is *never* in the table's
interests to mutually withdraw. [[edit: I still quite like this one.
The legitimate withdrawer still can without any changes - and I don't
think I've ever seen a game where two people withdraw for normal "I'm
out of deck, oh my god I have to get out here" reasons, vs rapid
withdrawal at the end of a game]]. The mutual throw down cards until we
all leave the game situation isn't possible. You could still, maybe,
bargain with someone so that they could withdraw to get a VP if they
help you but...]]

Again, this is not perfect. (Though a couple of them have a certain
sense of... something to them. I admit it's three in the morning,
though.) But what isn't it?

It's not telling players "These are the facts of the game, in-game.
This is how you would get the best out of the game. But you can't do
it."

Telling players that you, as the judge, have to deliberately curtail
the best play is inherently wrong.

If the "best play" is wrong for some reason, fix that.
***

It is really hard to withdraw when people want to stop you. It is really
easy to withdraw if there are two or three people who all agree to either
let you or mutually withdraw.

That it is difficult to withdraw on your own is good, but it is also good
that you can try--it gives incentive to go forward in a deadlock situation.

That it is easy to withdraw when everyone agrees to it doesn't strike me as
a problem at all.

I'm guessing what Orpheus is objecting to is people using Withdrawl as a
bargaining tool (i.e. "If you let me withdraw, I'll stop doing anything to
you as my prey..."), which is effectively a kind of table split deal, which
is kind of a problem. But as it goes, it is a very weak table split deal,
and is only legal if you aren't going to get any VPs otherwise. So I'm not
really seeing the problem there.

> If I
> wanted to argue it was a problem, I'd point out that aggressiveness, not
> passiveness should be rewarded.

That is exactly what the Withdrawl rule does. If you have 4 people all
deadlocked, and all out of deck, and someone tries to withdraw (which is a
reasonable thing to do, given that it gets oy umore VPs), the reward comes
from foiling the withdraw attempt. Being passive does not let you withdraw.
Your *opponents* being passive lets you withdraw.

In terms of deals, however, thta is a completely different issue, and I
think it is the deal issue that is objected to here. I would point out,
however, that the only difference in this situation between there being a
withdrawing rule and not is that people can finagle an extra .5 VP by making
a withdraw deal. Which is not even remotely a big deal in the grand scheme
of things.

> Of course the good counter to that
> argument is that it's pretty much impossible to get into a tournament
> finals with 3 VP except in the case of very small tournaments.

Especially given that in three games, you are giving someone different each
time a sweep by giving up for the 1 VP. I don't think the "You get 4 VP and
I get 1 'cause you let me withdraw" deal is even close to a winning one. And
likely isn't one that happens all that often, let alone frequently.

All I can think of as being what Orpheus is objecting to is the use of "let
me withdraw" as a bargaining chip. Usually, it is only going to be worth
your time to do that if you were getting zero VPs in any case, and if there
wasn't a withdraw rule, you could do the same thing by saying "let me time
the game out for the .5 VP..." which would be the exact same deal, except
for just .5 VP less.

Is it worth quibbling over the .5 VP?

> Could you also clarify how your previous example can be explained as the

> Did it make anyone try to oust someone when they wouldn't have if the rule
> didn't exist?

If your prey tries to withdraw, you need to go forward to stop them. Heck,
even if going forward consists of everyone going forward to bleed for one
just to keep their prey from withdrawing, that is more actions being taken
than if there was no withdrawing attempted.

And if people are taking actions to go forward, they are tapping minions and
getting in combat or bleeding folks. Eventually, some hole will break open
and something is bound to happen.

With no Withdraw rule, in a deadlock, everyone just sits and waits for time
to run out. With a Withdraw rule, in a deadlock, if someone is out of cards,
they can attempt to withdraw, forcing forward action. Sure, maybe not a lot
of forward action, but some, and maybe that is all that is necessary to get
the game going somewhere.

You don't get rewarded with 1 VP for making it to time. You get .5 VP for
making it to time. You get 1 VP for withdrawing, which you can only do if
everyone agrees on it or you are incredibly fortunate.

> However I do agree that it's an possible (if extremely rare) example
> of encouraging proactive play.

Extremely rare? I have been playing VTES competetively for a really long
time. Granted, this is totally anecdotal evidence (just like with Succubus
Club...), but in my life as a competetive VTES player, I have been involved
in exactly one game that ended with a three way mutual withdrawl (and I was
already ousted by then) by agreement. I have been involved in exactly zero
games where someone withdrew by virtue of a table split deal or something.
On the other hand, I have been in many, many games where someone ran out of
a deck and tried to withdraw simply 'cause they were out of a deck and
weren't going anywhere else soon, and the vast majority of the time, the
person trying to withdraw has failed, due to someone messing with them.

I really don't think that withdrawing comes up that much one way or the
other, and usually when it does, it is the result of simply someone trying
to withdraw 'cause they ran out of deck and it can't hurt to try.

I mean, ok, I really don't feel that strongly one way or the other about
this issue--if the Withdrawing rule was eliminated, I wouldn't really miss
it, as it really doesn't come up that often. But I am yet to be convinced
that it *needs* to be eliminated, as I have never seen it be disruptive (as
opposed, again, to Succubus Club, I say full well realizing the irony of
this statement :-). Yeah, I have seen a mass withdrawl occur a few times
(i.e., like 4 or 5 players in a deadlock all agreeing to mutually withdraw
and doing the monkey dance till their decks run out and then all
withdrawing), but pretty rarely, and a few of those time, the mass withdraw
was actually saving everyone's sanity in a game that everyone just wanted to
end.

There's quite a few prerequisites for withdrawal to actually encourage
someone to act against the withdrawee. Since you need:

A) A destabilizing deadlock where the position of the withdrawee is
becoming worse. (so that there's a reason someone would act against
him)
B) A situation where acting against the withdrawee is more attractive
than letting him withdraw.
C) A situation where acting against the withdrawee is bad for the
non-withdrawee acting against him. (so there's a reason he would
withdraw)

B is often more difficult to get than it seems imo. Time limit should
probably be around the corner (with a standard 2hr timelimit) and
there has to be a good reason why this person isn't acting against the
withdrawee.

IF B is fulfilled it is probably because the person acting against the
withdrawee thinks he will have a better chance to oust the withdrawee
soon. (since he had a good reason not to be acting against the
withdrawee) If thats the case, he most likely would've been trying to
oust soon anyway.

If that's not the case, the only reason I could think of to act
against the withdrawee, would be stalling the game to prevent the
withdrawee from getting 2 VP for the gamewin.

If he didn't have a good reason not to act against the withdrawee,
withdrawing (and thus spurring him into action) is just bad play upon
bad play IMO.

Because of these reasons, I think it (assuming good play) only
sometimes, very slightly, moves the proactive play to an earlier point
in time.

I'm not sure if I'd call that encouraging proactive play, as there has
to be proactive play looming in the (near)future to encourage someone
to act against someone withdrawing.

Interesting you would say that.

I thought that the "invention" of the Game Win system was to discourage
"suicidal" FFW decks (like weenie computer hacking) that are almost bound
to get 1-2 VPs on every table, but which cannot really sweep or reliably
score 3-4 VPs. The Praxis Seizure: Budapest held two weeks ago made me
think the rule over... ;) The fifth player had 2 / 6.5 while the sixth
had 1 / 8. From the perspective of the sixth player, who incidentally
had the third highest VP total, the Game Win rule smelled kind of fishy...
;)

You need 2 VPs for a possible, or 2.5+ for a sure game win. In my book
that means that once the usual required VPs for the finals reach about
7.5 VPs, Game Wins only differentiate between the distribution of the VPs
the player has gained. Because, a deck that can only make 1 or 2 VPs each
table will not even have a chance. We're talking about decks that _can_
make an average of 2.5 VPs each table.

However, instead of encouraging people to play to oust as much as possible,
the Game Win rule encourages people to be passive, make table split deals
or bring 3VP decks. I think that it might do the game some good to consider
abolishing the GW rule for 50+ player tournaments.
